claim: CRISPR adaptation immunizes bacteria and archaea against viruses.
source: CRISPR adaptation immunizes bacteria and archaea against viruses.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by the cited literature in the introduction.

claim: During adaptation, the Cas1-Cas2 complex integrates fragments of invader DNA as spacers in the CRISPR array.
source: During adaptation, the Cas1-Cas2 complex integrates fragments of invader DNA as spacers in the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Cas4 has been implicated in selection and processing of prespacer substrates for Cas1-Cas2.
source: Recently, an additional protein Cas4 has been implicated in selection and processing of prespacer substrates for Cas1-Cas2, although this mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cas4 interacts directly with Cas1-Cas2 forming a Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex that captures and processes prespacers prior to integration.
source: We show that Cas4 interacts directly with Cas1-Cas2 forming a Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex that captures and processes prespacers prior to integration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex contains two copies of Cas4 that closely interact with the two integrase active sites of Cas1.
source: Structural analysis of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex reveals two copies of Cas4 that closely interact with the two integrase active sites of Cas1, suggesting a mechanism for substrate handoff following processing.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex processes single-stranded DNA provided in cis or in trans with a double-stranded DNA duplex.
source: We also find that the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex processes single-stranded DNA provided in cis or in trans with a double-stranded DNA duplex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cas4 cleaves precisely upstream of PAM sequences.
source: Cas4 cleaves precisely upstream of PAM sequences, ensuring the acquisition of functional spacers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The CRISPR locus is programmed with 'spacer' sequences that are derived from foreign DNA and serve as a record of prior infection events.
source: Within this system, the CRISPR locus is programmed with 'spacer' sequences that are derived from foreign DNA and serve as a record of prior infection events (Bolotin et al., 2005; Mojica et al., 2005; Pourcel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The host adapts to an infection event when Cas proteins insert short fragments from the invader DNA as new spacers between repeating sequence elements within the CRISPR locus.
source: The host adapts to an infection event when Cas proteins insert short fragments from the invader DNA as new spacers between repeating sequence elements within the CRISPR locus (reviewed in Jackson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The CRISPR locus is transcribed and processed into short CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), which assemble with Cas proteins to form a RNA-guided surveillance complex.
source: The locus is transcribed and processed into short CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), which assemble with Cas proteins to form a RNA-guided surveillance complex (reviewed in Hochstrasser and Doudna, 2015; Charpentier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The surveillance complex recognizes the target bearing complementarity to the crRNA sequence and a Cas nuclease cleaves or degrades the target during the interference stage.
source: Finally, the surveillance complex recognizes the target bearing complementarity to the crRNA sequence and a Cas nuclease cleaves or degrades the target during the interference stage (reviewed in Marraffini, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The adaptation proteins Cas1 and Cas2 are conserved among most CRISPR systems.
source: Although the machinery and mechanisms involved in CRISPR interference are extremely diverse (Koonin et al., 2017), the adaptation proteins Cas1 and Cas2 are conserved among most CRISPR systems, suggesting a common molecular mechanism for acquiring spacers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cas1 and Cas2 form a heterohexameric complex that catalyzes spacer integration via two transesterification reactions.
source: Cas1 and Cas2 form a heterohexameric complex that catalyzes spacer integration via two transesterification reactions mediated by nucleophilic attack of the 3ʹ-hydroxyl on each strand of a double-stranded prespacer substrate at the phosphodiester backbone within the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Integration occurs at the first repeat in the CRISPR array, with one attack occurring between the upstream leader sequence and the repeat and the other occurring on the opposite strand between the repeat and first spacer within the array.
source: Integration occurs at the first repeat in the CRISPR array, with one attack occurring between the upstream leader sequence and the repeat and the other occurring on the opposite strand between the repeat and first spacer within the array (Arslan et al., 2014; Nuñez et al., 2015a; Rollie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The integration reactions result in the insertion of the prespacer between two single-strand repeats, and this gapped intermediate is repaired by host factors.
source: These reactions result in the insertion of the prespacer between two single-strand repeats, and this gapped intermediate is repaired by host factors (Ivančić-Baće et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The adaptation complex must capture and process longer fragments of DNA from the invader containing a flanking sequence called a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
source: In order to form a functional spacer, the adaptation complex must capture and process longer fragments of DNA from the invader containing a flanking sequence called a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) (Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PAM is an essential motif during target recognition by the surveillance complex and must be present next to the target in order for interference to occur.
source: The PAM is an essential motif during target recognition by the surveillance complex and must be present next to the target in order for interference to occur (Deveau et al., 2008; Redding et al., 2015; Sashital et al., 2012; Semenova et al., 2011; Sternberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PAM is not part of the spacer and must be removed from the prespacer prior to integration through a processing step.
source: However, the PAM is not part of the spacer and must be removed from the prespacer prior to integration through a processing step.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CRISPR adaptation.

claim: Integration must occur in the correct orientation to produce a crRNA that is complementary to the PAM-containing strand of the invader.
source: In addition, integration must occur in the correct orientation to produce a crRNA that is complementary to the PAM-containing strand of the invader.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CRISPR function.

claim: Cas4 is widespread in type I, II, and V CRISPR systems.
source: Cas4 is widespread in type I, II, and V systems (Hudaiberdiev et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of cas4 reduced the adaptation efficiency in in vivo studies.
source: In in vivo studies, deletion of cas4 reduced the adaptation efficiency (Li et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017) and resulted in the acquisition of non-functional spacers from regions that lacked a correct PAM (Almendros et al., 2019; Kieper et al., 2018; Shiimori et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of cas4 resulted in the acquisition of non-functional spacers from regions that lacked a correct PAM.
source: In in vivo studies, deletion of cas4 reduced the adaptation efficiency (Li et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017) and resulted in the acquisition of non-functional spacers from regions that lacked a correct PAM (Almendros et al., 2019; Kieper et al., 2018; Shiimori et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some CRISPR systems have two cas4 genes that work together to define the PAM, length and orientation of spacers.
source: Some systems have two cas4 genes that work together to define the PAM, length and orientation of spacers, suggesting that the two Cas4 proteins are involved in processing each end of the prespacer and that they may be present during integration (Shiimori et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cas4 is involved in PAM-dependent prespacer processing in vitro.
source: Similarly, in vitro studies have suggested that Cas4 is involved in PAM-dependent prespacer processing (Lee et al., 2018; Rollie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cas4 endonucleolytically cleaves PAM-containing 3ʹ-single-stranded overhangs that flank double-stranded prespacers.
source: Cas4 endonucleolytically cleaves PAM-containing 3ʹ-single-stranded overhangs that flank double-stranded prespacers (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cas4 cleavage activity is dependent on the presence of Cas1 and Cas2.
source: Importantly, Cas4 cleavage activity is dependent on the presence of Cas1 and Cas2, and Cas4 inhibits premature integration of unprocessed prespacers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cas4 inhibits premature integration of unprocessed prespacers.
source: Importantly, Cas4 cleavage activity is dependent on the presence of Cas1 and Cas2, and Cas4 inhibits premature integration of unprocessed prespacers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Direct biochemical and structural evidence for the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex has remained elusive prior to this study.
source: These observations suggest that Cas4 associates with the Cas1-Cas2 complex, although direct biochemical and structural evidence for this Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex remains elusive (Lee et al., 2018; Plagens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Cas1-Cas2 complex from type I-C is stabilized in the presence of dsDNA.
source: When Cas1 and Cas2 were incubated with the target DNA, the proteins eluted earlier as a single peak, while unassociated Cas2 eluted at the original elution volume (Figure 1B–C). These data indicate that the Cas1-Cas2 complex from type I-C is stabilized in the presence of dsDNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Cas4, Cas1 and Cas2 eluted in a single peak from the size-exclusion column when incubated with the CRISPR hairpin target.
source: Following incubation of equimolar amounts of each component, Cas4, Cas1 and Cas2 eluted in a single peak from the size-exclusion column (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with an earlier elution volume than the Cas1-Cas2-target sample (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complexes contained the hairpin target DNA.
source: Both Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complexes contained the hairpin target DNA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The formation of the higher-order Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex is stabilized by the presence of dsDNA substrates.
source: Together, these data suggest that the proteins directly interact with the hairpin target, and the formation of the higher-order complex is also stabilized by the presence of dsDNA substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A 22 Å three-dimensional reconstruction of the Cas1-Cas2 complex was determined.
source: For the Cas1-Cas2 complex, we determined a 22 Å three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Cas1-Cas2 EM density revealed clear C2 symmetry.
source: The EM density revealed clear C2 symmetry, which was enforced during the final 3D refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2 supplement 2A.

claim: The overall architecture of the type I-C Cas1-Cas2 complex is similar to that of the crystal structure of the type II-A Cas1-Cas2-prespacer complex from Enterococcus faecalis.
source: The structural models fit well, and the overall architecture of the complex was similar to that of the crystal structure of the type II-A Cas1-Cas2-prespacer complex from Enterococcus faecalis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2 supplement 3.

claim: The E. coli type I-E Cas1-Cas2-prespacer complex did not fit well in the Cas1-Cas2 density.
source: In contrast, the E. coli type I-E Cas1-Cas2-prespacer complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) did not fit well in the Cas1-Cas2 density, revealing that the architecture of type I-C Cas1-Cas2 may be more similar to type II-A than to another type I system (Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2 supplement 3C.

claim: A 20 Å 3D reconstruction of symmetrical Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 particles was determined.
source: For the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex, we determined a 20 Å 3D reconstruction of symmetrical particles enforcing C2 symmetry (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2 supplement 2B.

claim: The segmented density of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex reveals additional density corresponding to two molecules of Cas4.
source: The segmented density clearly reveals the base Cas1-Cas2 architecture, along with additional density corresponding to two molecules of Cas4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An asymmetrical Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex with 1:4:2 stoichiometry was observed.
source: A subset of these particles was refined as a separate 21 Å 3D reconstruction without symmetry enforced, revealing an asymmetrical Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex with 1:4:2 stoichiometry (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cas4 interacts with Cas1 but not Cas2 within the ternary complex.
source: In both the symmetrical and asymmetrical Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 reconstructions, the Cas4 and Cas1 densities are contiguous but Cas4 appears to be distinct from the Cas2 density (Figure 2B–C). This suggests that Cas4 interacts with Cas1 but not Cas2 within the ternary complex, similar to the tight interaction we have previously observed between Cas4 and Cas1 in the absence of Cas2 (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data shown in Figure 2B-C and supported by prior work.

claim: The interaction surface between Cas4-Cas1 appears to be different in the context of the binary and ternary complexes.
source: However, the interaction surface between Cas4-Cas1 appears to be different in the context of the binary and ternary complexes, suggesting that Cas4 and Cas1 may have two alternative modes of interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structural data.

claim: All four orientations of Cas4 in the structural model position the Cas4 active site with varying degrees of proximity (19–38 Å) to the Cas1 active sites.
source: All four orientations position the Cas4 active site with varying degrees of proximity (19–38 Å) to the Cas1 active sites that bind the 3ʹ-OH end of the prespacer in structures of Cas1-Cas2-prespacer (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D–E).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 2 supplement 4.

claim: The proximity between Cas4 and the Cas1 active site suggests that the product of Cas4 cleavage could transit to the integrase active sites following cleavage.
source: The proximity between Cas4 and the Cas1 active site suggests that the product of Cas4 cleavage could transit to the integrase active sites following cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing proximity of active sites.

claim: The Cas4 density lies along the same surface of Cas1 that is expected to interact with elements within the CRISPR array during half-site and full-site integration.
source: We also note that the Cas4 density lies along the same surface of Cas1 that is expected to interact with elements within the CRISPR array during half-site and full-site integration, based on crystal structures of these intermediates (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with crystal structures shown in Figure 2 supplement 5.

claim: Cas4 binding may be mutually exclusive with CRISPR binding along the repeat-binding surface.
source: Together, these observations suggest that Cas4 binding may be mutually exclusive with CRISPR binding along the repeat-binding surface, and that Cas4 may dissociate prior to integration.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex was successfully purified using a prespacer substrate.
source: Using a modified protocol (see Materials and methods), we were able to successfully purify a peak containing Cas4, Cas1, Cas2, and prespacer DNA from a size-exclusion column (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 supplement 2.

claim: The overall architecture of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2-prespacer complex is similar to complexes containing the hairpin target.
source: Although features are less well-defined for these lower resolution densities, the overall architecture is similar between the complexes containing the two different DNA substrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), indicating that complex formation occurs similarly regardless of the type of DNA substrate.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2 supplement 6.

claim: Cleavage product was observed for the ssDNA substrate in the presence of the CRISPR DNA.
source: Interestingly, for the ssDNA substrate, we observed cleavage product in the presence of the CRISPR DNA, while the DNA remained uncleaved in the absence of the CRISPR DNA or Cas4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Similar amounts of cleavage were observed for duplex prespacers with and without the CRISPR DNA.
source: However, we observed similar amounts of cleavage for duplex prespacers with and without the CRISPR, suggesting that the presence of the CRISPR DNA only enhances cleavage of the ssDNA substrate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both the ssDNA substrate and the duplex substrate produced the same length product.
source: Consistently, both the ssDNA substrate and the duplex substrate produced the same length product, suggesting they were cleaved at the PAM site located within the 3ʹ-overhang of the duplex substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 can cleave PAM sites in ssDNA when a CRISPR DNA is provided in trans.
source: These data suggest that Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 can cleave PAM sites in ssDNA when a CRISPR DNA is provided in trans, and that the dsDNA region present within the duplex prespacer is sufficient to stimulate complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: No integration product was visible for the single-stranded substrate following processing.
source: Notably, although the cleavage product for the duplex prespacer was integrated into the CRISPR (Figure 3B), no integration product was visible for the single-stranded substrate following processing even at increased image contrast (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 supplement 1B.

claim: Optimal integration requires that the single-stranded region be attached to a duplex.
source: Together, these results suggest that although Cas1 can integrate ssDNA, optimal integration requires that the single-stranded region be attached to a duplex, which may facilitate handoff of the processed end from Cas4 to the Cas1 active site.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The duplex substrate was cleaved within the single-stranded overhang region in the presence of Cas4.
source: As expected, the duplex substrate was cleaved within the single-stranded overhang region in the presence of Cas4, similar to the duplex substrate tested in Figure 3B (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For the ssDNA substrate, no cleavage was observed in the absence or at low concentrations of dsDNA, while cleavage product accumulated at higher dsDNA concentrations.
source: For the ssDNA substrate, no cleavage was observed in the absence or at low concentrations of dsDNA, while cleavage product accumulated at higher dsDNA concentrations (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Type I-C Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 adaptation complex can be stabilized by dsDNA.
source: Overall, our results show that type I-C Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 adaptation complex can be stabilized by dsDNA and that, within this complex, Cas4 is activated for ssDNA cleavage for substrate provided either in cis or in trans.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cas4 is activated for ssDNA cleavage within the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex for substrate provided either in cis or in trans.
source: Overall, our results show that type I-C Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 adaptation complex can be stabilized by dsDNA and that, within this complex, Cas4 is activated for ssDNA cleavage for substrate provided either in cis or in trans.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 precisely cleaved the ssDNA directly upstream of the PAM.
source: Comparison with ddNTP Sanger sequencing reactions revealed that Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 precisely cleaved the ssDNA directly upstream of the PAM, while Cas1-Cas2 or Cas4 alone failed to cleave the substrates (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: This cleavage site is consistent with the expected processing site relative to the PAM required to form a functional spacer during spacer acquisition.
source: This cleavage site is consistent with the expected processing site relative to the PAM required to form a functional spacer during spacer acquisition.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and knowledge of CRISPR function.

claim: Substrates with 10, 8, 6, 4 or 2-nt between three PAM sites generated three different sized cleavage products, resulting from cleavage directly upstream of each PAM site.
source: Substrates with 10, 8, 6, 4 or 2-nt between three PAM sites generated three different sized cleavage products, resulting from cleavage directly upstream of each PAM site (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4 supplement 1.

claim: When three PAM sites were introduced consecutively on ssDNA substrates, a predominant product was observed at the first PAM position.
source: However, when we introduced three PAM sites consecutively on ssDNA substrates, we observed a predominant product at the first PAM position (Figure 4C), indicating that processing was inhibited at the second and third PAM site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The adaptation complex can process multiple PAM sites within a single substrate as long as the PAMs are not consecutive.
source: Together, these results suggest that the adaptation complex can process multiple PAM sites within a single substrate as long as the PAMs are not consecutive.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All substrates with different PAM-flanking sequences displayed a single predominant cleavage product directly upstream of the PAM site.
source: Although we observed low levels of non-specific degradation in the presence of Cas4-Cas1-Cas2, all substrates displayed a single predominant cleavage product directly upstream of the PAM site (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Cas4 is highly PAM specific, as it did not cleave efficiently at other sites in the random sequences.
source: These results indicate that Cas4 is highly PAM specific, as it did not cleave efficiently at other sites in the random sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant differences were detected in relative sequence levels for the –Cas4 and +Cas4 samples in the degenerate sequence analysis.
source: We detected no significant differences in relative sequence levels for the –Cas4 and +Cas4 samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that all PAM-flanking sequences were cleaved with the same efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 supplement 1D-E.

claim: Cas4 cleavage specificity is dictated only by the presence of a PAM sequence within a single-stranded region of the substrate.
source: Together, our cleavage analyses strongly suggest that Cas4 cleavage specificity is dictated only by the presence of a PAM sequence within a single-stranded region of the substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The four different substrates with varying PAM positions yielded products of different lengths, indicating they were cleaved based on the position of the PAM within the single-stranded overhang.
source: The four different substrates yielded products of different lengths, indicating that they were cleaved based on the position of the PAM within the single-stranded overhang (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cas4 processed substrates with varying PAM positions to varying degrees.
source: Interestingly, Cas4 processed these substrates to varying degrees (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: The substrate in which the PAM was located close to the duplex (two nt between duplex and PAM site) was cleaved inefficiently.
source: The substrate in which the PAM was located close to the duplex (two nt between duplex and PAM site) was cleaved inefficiently, while the other three substrates were cleaved with similar efficiency (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The PAM must be located at a longer distance from the duplex to be accommodated within the Cas4 active site.
source: These data, along with prior results showing that Cas4 cannot cleave a PAM contained within a dsDNA (Lee et al., 2018), suggest that the PAM must be located at a longer distance from the duplex to be accommodated within the Cas4 active site.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6 and prior work.

claim: The presence of dsDNA substrates stabilizes the formation of both Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complexes in the B. halodurans type I-C system.
source: Here, we discovered that the presence of dsDNA substrates stabilizes the formation of both Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complexes in the B. halodurans type I-C system.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: The architecture of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex that mediates prespacer selection, processing, and integration during CRISPR adaptation is presented for the first time.
source: For the first time, we present the architecture of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex that mediates prespacer selection, processing, and integration during CRISPR adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by structural data in Figure 2.

claim: The structural analysis of B. halodurans type I-C adaptation complexes reveals a structure that is mutually exclusive with the previously determined Cas4-Cas1 complex.
source: Our structural analysis of B. halodurans type I-C adaptation complexes reveals a structure that is mutually exclusive with the previously determined Cas4-Cas1 complex (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structural data with prior work.

claim: In the Cas4-Cas1 complex, the two Cas1 dimers are in close proximity and would exclude the Cas2 dimer.
source: In the Cas4-Cas1 complex, the two Cas1 dimers are in close proximity and would exclude the Cas2 dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison with prior work.

claim: Cas4-Cas1 must fully dissociate in order for the Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex to form.
source: These results strongly suggest that Cas4-Cas1 must fully dissociate in order for the Cas1-Cas2 and Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex to form.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations.

claim: Some CRISPR systems contain Cas4-1 fusion proteins.
source: Interestingly, some systems contain Cas4-1 fusion proteins (Hudaiberdiev et al., 2017), and a recent study indicates that the Cas4 domain performs a similar function in prespacer processing within this fusion (Almendros et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Cas4 domain performs a similar function in prespacer processing within Cas4-1 fusion proteins.
source: Interestingly, some systems contain Cas4-1 fusion proteins (Hudaiberdiev et al., 2017), and a recent study indicates that the Cas4 domain performs a similar function in prespacer processing within this fusion (Almendros et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Fitting of structural models into the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 reconstruction suggests that Cas4 and Cas1 interact extensively and that their active sites may be in close proximity.
source: Our structural analysis of the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 complex provides further evidence toward this model. Fitting of structural models into the Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 reconstruction suggests that Cas4 and Cas1 interact extensively and that their active sites may be in close proximity.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cas4 may block binding of the ssDNA in the Cas1 active site prior to processing.
source: Thus, it is possible that Cas4 blocks binding of the ssDNA in the Cas1 active site prior to processing.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural observations.

claim: Other RecB-like nucleases bind single-stranded DNA by threading the substrate through a hole formed in the donut-shaped nuclease domain.
source: Other RecB-like nucleases bind single-stranded DNA by threading the substrate through a hole formed in the donut-shaped nuclease domain (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Similar binding by Cas4 may prevent release of the ssDNA until cleavage, at which point the upstream product would be released, allowing handoff to the Cas1 active site and enabling integration.
source: Similar binding by Cas4 may prevent release of the ssDNA until cleavage, at which point the upstream product would be released, allowing handoff to the Cas1 active site and enabling integration.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with other nucleases.

claim: Cas4 processing activity was independent of the duplex or overhang lengths in previous studies.
source: Previously, we showed that Cas4 processes prespacers with duplexes flanked by 3ʹ overhangs, and that processing activity was independent of the duplex or overhang lengths (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Interactions of the prespacer duplex along the length of the Cas1-Cas2 core anchors the substrate to the complex, facilitating efficient Cas4 cleavage and direct handoff of the 3ʹ overhangs from Cas4 to Cas1.
source: These results suggest that interactions of the prespacer duplex along the length of the Cas1-Cas2 core anchors the substrate to the complex, facilitating efficient Cas4 cleavage and direct handoff of the 3ʹ overhangs from Cas4 to Cas1.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the absence of the cis duplex, the ssDNA is likely to be released by the complex upon Cas4 cleavage due to the lack of an anchoring interaction with the complex.
source: In the absence of the cis duplex, the ssDNA is likely to be released by the complex upon Cas4 cleavage due to the lack of an anchoring interaction with the complex.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: A duplex DNA containing single-strand overhangs is likely the optimal Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 substrate to enable efficient cleavage and substrate handoff.
source: Therefore, a duplex DNA containing single-strand overhangs is likely the optimal Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 substrate to enable efficient cleavage and substrate handoff.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: It remains unclear how prespacers with duplex DNA containing single-strand overhangs are formed.
source: It remains unclear how these types of prespacers are formed.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: In other CRISPR-Cas sub-types, Cas4 has been demonstrated to have exonucleolytic activity that can lead to dsDNA unwinding.
source: In other CRISPR-Cas sub-types, Cas4 has been demonstrated to have exonucleolytic activity that can lead to dsDNA unwinding (Lemak et al., 2013; Lemak et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012), although we have not observed robust exonuclease or dsDNA cleavage activity for the type I-C BhCas4 (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Robust exonuclease or dsDNA cleavage activity has not been observed for the type I-C BhCas4.
source: In other CRISPR-Cas sub-types, Cas4 has been demonstrated to have exonucleolytic activity that can lead to dsDNA unwinding (Lemak et al., 2013; Lemak et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012), although we have not observed robust exonuclease or dsDNA cleavage activity for the type I-C BhCas4 (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Other host factors or conditions may be required to unwind ends of dsDNA, or to expose single-stranded overhangs for precise cleavage by Cas4 in the type I-C system.
source: It is possible that other host factors or conditions are required to unwind ends of dsDNA, or to expose single-stranded overhangs for precise cleavage by Cas4 in the type I-C system.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observations.

claim: Cas4 processing can occur at several locations within both trans and cis ssDNA, as long as enough space is available between cleavage sites and the end of a duplex.
source: Surprisingly, Cas4 processing can occur at several locations within both trans and cis ssDNA, as long as enough space is available between cleavage sites and the end of a duplex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Cas4-dependent PAM processing is not observed in the absence of Cas1-Cas2.
source: Importantly, we do not observe Cas4-dependent PAM processing in the absence of Cas1-Cas2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Once activated, Cas4 can sample any region of a single-stranded DNA that is accessible to the active site.

evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: The ability of Cas4 to search for PAM sequences within single-stranded overhangs could allow more flexibility in defining prespacer substrates.

evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 only processes the PAM-proximal end in type I-C.
source: In these experiments, Cas4 did not appear to have strong cleavage activity at non-PAM sites, suggesting that Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 only processes the PAM-proximal end in type I-C.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In type I-A from Pyrococcus furiousus, two distinct Cas4 proteins coordinate the processing of each end of the prespacer.
source: In type I-A from Pyrococcus furiousus, two distinct Cas4 proteins coordinate the processing of each end of the prespacer (Shiimori et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most Cas4-containing systems, including type I-C, lack a second cas4 gene.
source: However, most Cas4-containing systems, including type I-C, lack a second cas4 gene.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of CRISPR system organization.

claim: In systems lacking a second cas4 gene, Cas4 may define the PAM-distal end of the prespacer through an alternative cleavage activity or another host factor may be required for this processing activity.
source: It is possible that in these systems, Cas4 may define the PAM-distal end of the prespacer through an alternative cleavage activity or that another host factor is required for this processing activity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observations.

claim: Formation of functional spacers requires that the PAM end of the prespacer must be integrated at the leader-distal end of the repeat following prespacer processing.
source: Formation of functional spacers requires that the PAM end of the prespacer must be integrated at the leader-distal end of the repeat following prespacer processing.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of CRISPR function.

claim: The precise details of how spacer orientation is defined during integration remain unknown.
source: The precise details of how spacer orientation is defined during integration remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: In type I-E, one nucleotide of the PAM is retained following prespacer processing, and this nucleotide may help to define the PAM end during integration.
source: In type I-E, one nucleotide of the PAM is retained following prespacer processing, and this nucleotide may help to define the PAM end during integration (Datsenko et al., 2012; Swarts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the type I-A system, the two Cas4 proteins are required to define orientation.
source: In the type I-A system, the two Cas4 proteins are required to define orientation (Shiimori et al., 2018), suggesting that their presence in an adaptation complex may define the orientation of the spacer after the prespacer is fully processed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The asymmetrical complex containing only one Cas4 subunit may define prespacer orientation.
source: Notably, we observed asymmetrical complexes of Cas4-Cas1-Cas2 containing only one Cas4 subunit. This configuration, along with the hypothesis that Cas4 only processes the PAM end of the prespacer, could suggest that only a single copy of Cas4 is required to form a functional adaptation complex. Indeed, the asymmetrical complex may also define prespacer orientation, based on which end of the prespacer is bound at the Cas4-end of the complex.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural observations.

claim: Only a single copy of Cas4 may be required to form a functional adaptation complex.
source: This configuration, along with the hypothesis that Cas4 only processes the PAM end of the prespacer, could suggest that only a single copy of Cas4 is required to form a functional adaptation complex.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural observations.

claim: The structural model indicates that Cas4 may be mutually exclusive with binding at the CRISPR array.
source: Our structural model also indicates that Cas4 may be mutually exclusive with binding at the CRISPR array (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that the end of the asymmetrical complex lacking Cas4 may preferentially bind to the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations shown in Figure 2 supplement 5.

claim: Integration occurs first at the leader-end of the repeat.
source: We previously showed that integration occurs first at the leader-end of the repeat (Lee et al., 2018), which is also the site of integration for the non-PAM end of the prespacer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: An asymmetrical complex may define spacer orientation by ensuring that the non-PAM end is integrated first.
source: Thus, it is possible that an asymmetrical complex may define spacer orientation by ensuring that the non-PAM end is integrated first.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observations.
